title: Part II – Microstructural and mechanical characterization of additively manufactured components of 18Ni300M steel with gas and water-atomized powders: a comparative study between aged PBF-LB and conventional material focused on the fatigue behavior
abstract: Abstract Maraging 300 (18Ni300M) steel is a ferrous alloy renowned for its good combination of mechanical strength and ductility, making it ideal for aerospace and defense applications. A previous study demonstrated that the atomization process has a significant influence on the monotonic mechanical properties and microstructure of as-built components produced by powder bed fusion with a laser beam (PBF-LB) technique. In Part II, the tensile and high-cycle fatigue behavior of 18Ni300M steel aged at 480 ºC for 3 h was investigated across two processing routes: conventional vacuum induction melting followed by vacuum arc remelting (VIM/VAR), and PBF-LB using gas-atomized (GA) and water-atomized (WA) powders. The research included tensile and rotary bending fatigue tests, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for nanoparticle analysis, and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) for identifying secondary microcrack paths. The results showed that aging increased the mechanical strength of both GA and VIM/VAR samples, albeit with a reduction in ductility. In contrast, the WA condition exhibited compromised plasticity, as oxide inclusions acted as critical-size defects. The VIM/VAR specimens demonstrated the highest fatigue resistance, followed by the GA condition, which was limited by nano-oxide formation and process-induced defects. The WA specimens displayed the lowest fatigue performance due to a greater number of defects exceeding the critical defect size predicted by Murakami’s model. These findings highlight the influence of powder characteristics, processing routes, and microstructural features on the mechanical properties of an ultra-high-strength steel intended for structural applications.
journal: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Maraging 300 steel containing 18 wt.% nickel, also referred to as 18Ni300M steel, is an ultra-high-strength steel characterized by a favorable balance between fracture toughness (K Ic  = 80 MPa∙m 0.5 ) and mechanical strength (YS = 300 ksi ≈ 2000 MPa) [ 1 ]. This combination of properties renders the alloy suitable for the nuclear, naval, defense, aerospace, die-casting, and tooling industries [ 1 ,  2 ]. This type of steel is composed of a ductile martensitic matrix with intermetallic precipitates dispersed throughout that are formed during the aging heat treatment [ 3 ,  4 ]. The high nickel content in 18Ni300M steel provides high strength and austenite stability [ 5 ], while the addition of cobalt and molybdenum enhances its resistance to thermal and mechanical degradation [ 6 ,  7 ].

The precipitation of nanometric intermetallics, such as Ni 3 Mo, Ni 3 Ti, their compositional variants, and Laves phases, represents the primary hardening mechanism governing the mechanical properties of 18Ni300M steel [ 8 ,  9 ]. The size, shape, and distribution of the precipitates and resulting mechanical properties depend on the temperature and duration of aging heat treatment. For example, Ni 3 Mo, Ni 3 Ti, and Ni 3 (Mo,Ti) are the first precipitates formed during aging at 480 ºC [ 10 ]. As time and temperature increase, these compounds tend to coarsen and become less effective at impeding dislocation movement or may even decompose [ 11 ].

There is a growing interest in processing engineering materials like 18Ni300M steel using innovative, cost-effective, and environmentally friendly methodologies, such as additive manufacturing (AM) [ 12 ,  13 ]. Powder bed fusion with a laser beam (PBF-LB) is an AM process that utilizes a high-powered laser to fuse particulate raw material. By melting powder particles layer by layer, PBF-LB can create intricate and complex 3D parts [ 14 ]. PBF-LB has demonstrated the ability to produce dense, strong, and thermodynamically stable parts when applied to 18Ni300M steel [ 15 ,  16 ]. Given the maturity of the process for this alloy, extensive research has focused on understanding the solidification microstructure formed during the AM process [ 17 ], as well as the mechanisms of precipitation and austenite reversion during heat treatments [ 5 ]. In addition, investigations have explored the relationship between the as-built and heat-treated microstructures and their impact on mechanical properties, including those determined through fatigue tests [ 18 ,  19 ].

Fatigue studies are typically classified into three categories: high-cycle fatigue (HCF), low-cycle fatigue (LCF), and fatigue crack growth (FCG). Fatigue generally results from plastic deformation caused by cyclic strains at grain boundaries, which can initiate and propagate cracks [ 20 ]. HCF is predominantly observed in materials subjected to numerous loading cycles, where elastic deformation prevails, and plastic deformation is localized at specific points. This behavior is common to components such as turbine blades and automotive parts, which represent potential applications for 18Ni300M steel [ 2 ]. When this alloy is produced via conventional manufacturing methods, e.g., vacuum induction melting and vacuum arc remelting (VIM/VAR), it demonstrates considerable HCF strength. For example, in axial tension–compression fatigue tests (R = − 1), VIM/VAR-aged samples subjected to heat treatment at 480 ºC for 3 h exhibited a fatigue strength of 700 MPa, reaching approximately 10 6  to 10 7  cycles [ 21 ]. This performance makes maraging steel particularly well-suited for different applications. However, it is important to note that factors such as applied stresses, environmental conditions, and the fabrication process can influence its fatigue resistance [ 22 ].

Studies have investigated the HCF properties of 18Ni300M steel fabricated using the PBF-LB technique. After undergoing aging heat treatment at 490 ºC for 6 h, specimens subjected to rotary bending fatigue tests exhibited fatigue strengths ranging from 460 to 550 MPa within 10 6  to 10 7  cycles [ 23 ]. Materials produced through AM often inherit defects from the fabrication process, such as porosity and lack of fusion. These defects can serve as sites prone to crack nucleation and growth, contributing to increased variability and dispersion in fatigue performance [ 24 ].

In addition to manufacturing methods, the nature of the feedstock powder can be a critical variable influencing the properties of parts produced via PBF-LB. In a previous study, our group observed that gas-atomized (GA) and water-atomized (WA) 18Ni300M steel powders yielded as-built specimens with similar tensile strength but different ductility [ 25 ]. Specifically, specimens processed from the WA batch exhibited an elongation to fracture of 4.06%, approximately three times lower than those produced from the GA batch. Regarding the fatigue behavior of 18Ni300M steel and the atomization methods used to make powders for PBF-LB, a study investigated vacuum inert gas atomization (VIGA) and inert gas atomization (IGA) processes [ 26 ]. These methods resulted in powders with different oxygen and nitrogen contents, with VIGA powders exhibiting lower levels of these impurities than IGA powders. Consequently, the fatigue strength of the VIGA batch reached approximately 700 MPa, whereas the IGA batch achieved 570 MPa. This difference was attributed to the higher volume fraction of non-metallic inclusions, such as TiN and oxides rich in Ti and Al, dispersed in the microstructure of the IGA material.

The primary objective of this study is to compare the high-cycle fatigue and tensile behavior of 18Ni300M steel processed by PBF-LB using gas-atomized (GA) and water-atomized (WA) powders with that of material produced by the conventional vacuum induction melting and vacuum arc remelting (VIM/VAR) route. Additionally, the indirect effects of aging heat treatment performed at 480 ºC for 3 h on these mechanical properties and the resulting microstructures are evaluated. To achieve this, SEM, XEDS, EBSD, and TEM analyses were conducted to elucidate the influence of secondary phases within the microstructures, identify micromechanisms of fracture during monotonic and cyclic tests, and specifically investigate the presence of secondary microcracks in HCF samples. While the first part of this research builds upon a previously published study by the group [ 25 ], the majority of the present article provides new insights into the impact of aging and microstructural defects on the mechanical behavior of an ultra-high-strength steel designed for demanding aerospace and military applications. This approach advances the understanding of how powder characteristics and heat treatments influence the performance of additively manufactured 18Ni300M steel.

sections.heading: Alloy processing, printing quality evaluation, and direct aging heat treatment
paragraphs: Two batches of 18Ni300M steel raw material were separately processed using the PBF-LB technique: N 2  gas-atomized (GA) and water-atomized (WA) powders, which were characterized in a previous study conducted by our research group [ 25 ]. A summary of the main characterizations performed on the GA and WA powders is presented in Table  1 . For a more detailed discussion and full characterization results, readers can refer to our previous publication elsewhere [ 25 ]. An EOS M280 manufacturing system was used to process GA and WA 18Ni300M steel parts via PBF-LB under a nitrogen-protective atmosphere. From a macroscopic perspective, no significant differences were observed between the components produced from the two powder batches regarding solidification cracks, adherence of sacrificial powder to the surface, or coloration. The laser power was set between 180 and 200 W, with a beam spot diameter ranging from 100 to 120 μm, a scanning speed of 1 m/s, a hatch distance of 100 μm and a layer thickness of 50 μm were maintained throughout the process [ 28 ]. Based on the specified parameters, the estimated volumetric energy density for the PBF-LB processing was 40 J/mm 3 . A relative rotation of 67º was applied between the scan lines of consecutive layers. A brief assessment of the printing quality of as-built (AB) parts processed by AM using GA and WA powder batches was conducted in the referred study [ 25 ]. This evaluation involved the determination of the surface porosity fraction in optical micrographs through quantitative stereology theory, and the density measurement via the Archimedes method [ 29 ]. Using YZ-section micrographs from reference [ 25 ] and the freeware ImageJ [ 27 ], the average melt pool depth of the fabricated parts was measured to compare the behavior of GA and WA batches, focusing on how their oxygen content indirectly influences surface tension in the liquid metal pool and, then, affects melt pool depth.

On the other hand, conventional maraging steel was produced by VIM/VAR processes as a 10 mm thick plate and provided for studies by the Department of Aerospace Science and Technology (DCTA, Brazil) [ 30 ].

The 18Ni300M steel samples were isothermally heat-treated at 480 ºC for 3 h in a Kanthal muffle-type resistive furnace, as schematically illustrated in Fig.  1 (a). Fig. 1 ( a ) Schematic representation of the isothermal heat treatment performed at 480 ºC for 3 h on 18Ni300M steel samples processed through PBF-LB and VIM/VAR methods. The samples were directly aged without undergoing annealing heat treatment. ( b ) Orthographic view of the specimens prepared for rotary bending fatigue tests. The z-axis corresponds to the building direction (BD) in PBF-LB or the rolling direction (RD) in conventionally processed samples. SD denotes the scanning direction in the PBF-LB process, while TD refers to the transverse direction relative to SD. All dimensions are in millimeters

No annealing heat treatment was performed on the samples processed by PBF-LB or through the VIM/VAR routes to specifically assess the effect of direct aging on the microstructure and properties of the materials. After the heat treatment, the samples were air-cooled to room temperature. The selected aging condition is based on one of the most commonly applied heat treatments for 18Ni300M steel in both industrial and academic contexts [ 11 ,  21 ], as it promotes optimized precipitation of intermetallic phases at this temperature and duration [ 2 ].

sections.heading: Microstructure and hardness characterization
paragraphs: The PBF-LB as-built (AB), VIM/VAR as-fabricated (AF), and aged (A) specimens of both processing routes were prepared by grinding with silicon carbide (SiC) emery paper ranging from 320 to 2400 grit sizes. The samples were polished using a 0.05 μm silica suspension following the ASTM E3 standard. A 5% nitric acid solution mixed with ethanol was applied for etching for 10 to 30 s. Microstructural analysis, including image acquisition and X-ray energy dispersive spectroscopy (XEDS) mapping, was performed using a Thermo Fisher Scientific Quanta 650 FEG microscope at the Brazilian Nanotechnology National Laboratory (LNNano) of the Brazilian National Laboratory (CNPEM) and a Thermo Scientific Quattro scanning electron microscope at the Center for Electron Microscopy and Analysis (CEMAS) of the Ohio State University (OSU). Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analyses were conducted on the same OSU/CEMAS microscope equipped with an EDAX Velocity camera. EBSD data collection parameters included an acceleration voltage of 20 kV, a step size of 0.25 μm, and an exposure time of 0.3 s. The EBSD data were processed using the MTEX software [ 31 ].

To investigate the chemical composition of nanoparticles dispersed within the microstructure of aged GA batch-processed parts, high-magnification scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging and XEDS line scan were performed under specific conditions: a small aperture (number 6), a short working distance (5 mm), and a high acceleration voltage (20 kV). These parameters were selected to enhance spatial resolution and minimize diffraction effects while enabling elemental analysis along a defined profile line. Although signal interaction with underlying phases may occur at 20 kV, the selected approach allowed for a preliminary compositional assessment of the particles. However, due to the small size of the nanoparticles investigated, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) combined with XEDS was employed to determine their composition accurately. For this purpose, a GA-aged sample was thinned using the focused ion beam (FIB) technique to a final thickness of approximately 50 nm, utilizing a dual-beam FEI Helios NanoLab 600 system (OSU/CEMAS). Before TEM analysis, organic material and other residues from the FIB preparation were removed by plasma cleaning. High-resolution TEM imaging was performed using a Thermo Scientific Themis Z S/TEM (OSU/CEMAS) operated at 300 kV, in high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) mode with a fifth-order aberration-corrected probe. Elemental analyses were carried out on the same instrument using XEDS.

Vickers hardness measurements were performed at ten random locations following the ASTM E384-17 standard. A load of 200 gf was applied for 15 s to 18Ni300M steel samples polished with a 0.05 μm silica suspension.

sections.heading: Tensile tests
paragraphs: Tensile tests were performed on 18Ni300M steel in as-built and heat-treated conditions using an MTS 810.23 M machine with displacement control. An MTS model 632.26F-21 extensometer with a gauge length of 8.0 mm was used for strain measurement during the experiments. The tests were conducted at a speed of 0.5 mm/min, and data were collected at a rate of 4 points per second. The subsized specimens used for the tests were based on references [ 32 ,  33 ]. The monotonic mechanical properties of 18Ni300M steel, including yield stress (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS), and percent elongation, were determined as the average of three tests for each condition, following the ASTM E8/E8 M-1 standard.

sections.heading: High-cycle fatigue tests
paragraphs: The fatigue tests were conducted on 18Ni300M steel specimens heat-treated at 480 ºC for 3 h, processed either by PBF-LB using GA and WA powders, or through conventional means (VIM/VAR). The additively manufactured specimens were fabricated with the gauge section oriented at 0º relative to the building plate of the PBF-LB equipment, meaning that the longitudinal axis of the specimen was parallel to the top plane of the building plate and perpendicular to the building direction, following the configuration reported for the 0º condition in [ 34 ]. For comparison, VIM/VAR coupons were oriented along the rolling direction. All specimens were subsequently machined to achieve a test section average diameter of 3.03 ± 0.03 mm, as detailed in Fig.  1 (b). For the rotary bending cantilever beam fatigue tests conducted at room temperature, a Fatigue Dynamics RBF 200 machine was employed. Initial test load parameters were defined using the estimation method outlined by Lee et al. [ 35 ], which determines fatigue strength at 10 3  and 10 6  cycles, representing the onset of high-cycle fatigue and the fatigue life limit, respectively. The maximum loading was applied at a stress level corresponding to 90% of the UTS of the conventionally processed material. Stresses were progressively reduced in subsequent tests until a level where the material could sustain a life of 10 6  cycles. For the aged GA-PBF-LB processed material, the initial stress approximately matched the fatigue life threshold determined for the conventionally processed condition. The initial stress for the GA condition was set at approximately 1200 MPa, while for the WA batch, the initial stress was approximately 60% of that of the GA batch, i.e., around 700 MPa.

In this model, σ represents the applied nominal stress, which, in the rotary bending fatigue tests with R = − 1, is equivalent to the stress amplitude,  A  denotes a constant expressed in MPa, N f  represents the number of cycles to failure, and  b  characterizes the slope of the fatigue curve in a log–log plot, reflecting the rate at which fatigue life decreases as the applied stress increases [ 39 ].

sections.heading: Fractographic analysis
paragraphs: Fractographic image acquisition and XEDS mapping of the tensile and fatigue-tested 18Ni300M steel specimens were carried out using a Thermo Fisher Scientific Quanta 650 FEG microscope at LNNano/CNPEM and a Tescan Mira 4 field emission gun (FEG) SEM at the Engineering School of Lorena of the University of São Paulo. Two representative tensile-tested specimens (AB/AF and A) from each processing route, i.e., GA, WA, and VIM/VAR, were examined to compare the fracture micromechanisms and to assess the effects of the aging heat treatment on the fracture surfaces relative to the as-built and as-fabricated conditions.

sections.heading: Printing quality in PBF-LB GA and WA 18Ni300M steel parts
paragraphs: Table  2  presents the main results of the quality assessment of 18Ni300M steel parts processed by PBF-LB using GA and WA batches, summarizing findings from the previous study and the average melt pool depth measurements obtained from YZ-section micrographs, also shown in reference [ 25 ]. Table 2 Parameters investigated to assess the quality of 18Ni300M steel parts processed by PBF-LB using GA and WA batches: density determined by quantitative stereology and the Archimedes method, as well as the average melt pool depth [ 25 ] Batch Quantitative stereology Archimedes method Melt pool depth  (μm) GA 99.7% 99.3% 52.8 ± 2.8 WA 99.2% 99.0% 65.7 ± 2.6

The density results of PBF-LB 18Ni300M steel, as presented in Table  2 , indicate a similarity between the GA and WA batches, with no significant differences observed across the measurement methods employed, i.e., quantitative stereology and Archimedes’ principle [ 25 ]. Furthermore, the average melt pool depth in material processed from the WA batch is greater but remains within the range reported in the literature (50–100 μm) [ 1 ]. This outcome aligns with the findings of Pinkerton and Li [ 40 ], who demonstrated that increasing the morphological irregularity of powder particles, as shown in Table  1 , leads to a more chaotic molten metal flow. Additionally, the high oxygen concentration in parts processed from WA powder, also exhibited in Table  1 , influences the Marangoni effect [ 41 ]. In other words, oxygen acts as a surfactant in the molten metal, increasing surface tension as the temperature rises, which drives the liquid metal deeper into the substrate, ultimately resulting in deeper melt pools [ 14 ].

It is important to note that this paper represents a continuation of the first part of the characterization of components processed from GA and WA powder batches. In the previous study, the concentrations of all chemical elements listed in Table  1  were determined by optical emission spectroscopy, except for nitrogen (N) and oxygen (O), which were measured using wet chemical analysis. However, as previously reported [ 25 ], accurately quantifying these two nonmetals can be a challenge. Therefore, in the present study, the concentrations of N and O were remeasured in triplicate using inert gas fusion spectroscopy, performed on a LECO TL-600 system at the Department of Materials Science and Engineering at the Ohio State University (OSU). The nitrogen content obtained by both methods was nearly identical. In contrast, oxygen content results differed, particularly for the GA batch. The oxygen concentration determined via wet chemical analysis for the GA material was unrealistically low, about ten times lower than typical values reported for maraging 300 steel produced by the plasma rotating electrode process (PREP) [ 42 ], and nearly identical to that of conventionally processed VIM/VAR maraging steel [ 43 ]. Since both PREP and VIM/VAR introduce less oxygen into the material compared to PBF-LB, the oxygen levels measured via inert gas fusion spectroscopy are considered more representative. The underestimation observed in the wet chemical analysis is likely due to its limited ability to dissolve and react with nanometric oxide particles. These oxides may not have been fully converted into detectable chemical species, such as OH –  or H 2 O 2 , during the dissolution process. Additionally, this technique is not specifically optimized for oxygen determination in steels [ 44 ]. In contrast, inert gas fusion spectroscopy, designed for oxygen analysis in steels, enables quantification by melting the sample in a graphite crucible under an inert gas flow. The oxygen present in the sample reacts with the carbon in the crucible to form CO and CO 2 , which are then detected with high sensitivity via infrared absorption cells. That is the reason why this method provides a more realistic measurement of the total oxygen content in the GA batch, including both oxide particles and oxygen dissolved in the matrix [ 45 ]. The underestimated result observed for the WA batch is also supported by the same considerations. However, this does not affect any of the discussions in either part of the research, nor does it alter the fact that the components produced with the WA batch contain significantly higher oxygen levels than those manufactured with the GA batch.

sections.heading: 18Ni300M steel microstructures
paragraphs: Figure  2  displays IPF maps and micrographs of 18Ni300M steel in the as-built (AB) state processed by AM, in the as-fabricated (AF) condition through the VIM/VAR route, and aged (A) at 480 ºC for 3 h. The first column presents the IPF maps and microstructures of the 18Ni300M steel processed from GA powder in the AB and A conditions. The exact sequence of figures is maintained in the next two columns for the WA and VIM/VAR batches, respectively, clarifying that the first micrograph in the third column corresponds to the AF condition of the conventionally processed material. The IPF maps in Fig.  2 (a) and (b) show that samples processed by PBF-LB exhibit grains with a high aspect ratio, reflecting the morphology of the parental austenite formed during processing. In contrast, the IPF map in Fig.  2 (c) reveals a martensitic microstructure organized into packets containing distinct blocks in the AF material [ 2 ], a characteristic also visible in the microstructure of Fig.  2 (f). Fig. 2 IPF maps and microstructures of 18Ni300M steel processed by PBF-LB with a gas-atomized powder in the ( a ) and ( d ) as-built and ( g ) aged conditions and with a water-atomized powder in the ( b ) and ( e ) as-built and ( h ) aged states. Conventional 18Ni300M steel ( c ) IPF map and ( f ) as-fabricated and ( i ) aged microstructures

Micrographs in Fig.  2 (d) and (e) show the solidification microstructure typical of the PBF-LB process in the AB condition of GA and WA batches, respectively. Some differences include the presence of residual powder particles in the WA microstructure, which exhibit a gray tone very similar to that of the solidification cell boundaries, as indicated in Fig.  2 (e). Additionally, rounded black sites, also highlighted in Fig.  2 (e), are observed in the water-atomized microstructure and can be associated with second-phase particles. In the aged condition, Fig.  2 (g) and (h) demonstrate that both GA and WA batches retain the cellular solidification microstructure following the heat treatment. In contrast, the aged conventional alloy exhibits a pronounced block structure within each martensitic packet, as observed in Fig.  2 (i).

To determine the chemical nature of the circular sections observed in the microstructure of the material processed from the WA powder, XEDS maps were collected in both the as-built and aged conditions. The results indicate that the black circles are second-phase particles rich in oxygen, aluminum, silicon, and titanium, as shown in Fig.  3 (a)-(c). Fig. 3 XEDS maps of WA 18Ni300M steel are depicted in ( c ) for ( a ) as-built and ( b ) aged conditions, demonstrating that the particles observed in the microstructure are oxides; ( d ) and ( e ) aluminum nano-oxides present in the microstructure of aged 18Ni300M steel processed from GA powder

Analyzing the microstructures of the GA material, i.e., Fig.  2 (d) and (g), no second-phase particles are observed, unlike those found in the WA steel microstructure. However, literature and Table  1  indicate that the oxygen concentration in 18Ni300M steel parts produced by additive methods is sufficiently high for oxide formation [ 46 ,  47 ]. Given this, high-magnification SEM and XEDS analysis of the aged GA material microstructure, conducted under the conditions detailed in the methodology section, enabled the identification of nano-oxide particles enriched in aluminum and oxygen, as shown in Fig.  3 (d) and (e). However, due to the small size of the nanoparticles, TEM and XEDS analyses were performed on an aged lamella from the GA batch. The results, shown in Fig.  4 , reveal that the nanoparticles are distributed throughout the microstructure and are compositionally rich in aluminum, titanium, and oxygen. Additionally, regions exhibiting segregation of nickel, titanium, and molybdenum were observed. This phenomenon suggests the presence of intermetallic precipitates with dimensions smaller than those of the investigated nanoparticles [ 48 ]. Fig. 4 ( a ), ( b ), and ( e ) TEM-HAADF images at different magnifications for aged 18Ni300M steel lamella processed from the GA batch; ( c ) XEDS line scan along a 150 nm path, with ( d ) the corresponding variation in atomic fraction of Ni, Mo, and Ti as a function of position; ( f ) XEDS elemental maps for Al, Ti, and O; and ( g ) variation in the atomic fraction of the selected elements within one of the analyzed particles

sections.heading: Tensile properties
paragraphs: The engineering stress–strain curves for the aged 18Ni300M steel are shown in Fig.  5 . The corresponding curves for the as-built (PBF-LB using GA and WA batches) and as-fabricated (VIM/VAR) conditions can be found in the reference [ 25 ]. The properties extracted from the curves, along with Vickers hardness measurements and their respective deviations, are summarized in Table  3 . The mechanical properties of AB and AF states shown in Table  3  were initially presented in our previous publication [ 25 ] and are included here to facilitate comparison for the reader. In general, it can be observed that aging heat treatment enhances the mechanical strength, e.g., HV, YS, and UTS, of the GA and VIM/VAR alloys but reduces their ductility. Additionally, Fig.  5  shows that the plasticity of the aged samples processed from the WA batch was compromised, which will be discussed in the following section. Fig.  6 (a)-(f) show the fracture surfaces of representative tensile-tested specimens from each processing condition. For the GA and VIM/VAR batches in both the as-built/as-fabricated and aged conditions, shown in Fig.  6 (a) and (b), and (e) and (f), respectively, the reduction in ductility is evidenced by the presence of shallower dimples and the appearance of cleavage-like facets in the heat-treated fracture surfaces. In contrast, Fig.  6 (c) and (d) reveal that the fracture micromechanisms of the AB condition for the WA batch were already more brittle even before aging, as indicated by the presence of smaller and shallower dimples, likely due to the presence of constituent particles acting as microscopic stress raisers, such as those visible in Fig.  6 (c). Figure  6 (d), which presents a low-magnification image, shows a relatively flat fracture surface with embedded particles, one of which is outlined by a rectangle, whose XEDS analysis revealed high concentrations of oxygen and titanium. A higher-magnification image also shows flat facets, within which small regions of dimples are observed. Fig. 6 Fracture surfaces of representative tensile 18Ni300M steel samples from the GA, WA, and VIM/VAR batches in the AB/AF states: ( a ), ( c ), and ( e ), and in the A condition: ( b ), ( d ), and ( f ), respectively. The insets show magnified views of the areas marked by rectangles, and the XEDS map in ( d ) corresponds to a particle rich in oxygen and titanium

sections.heading: Fatigue behavior
paragraphs: Figure  7  shows the S–N curves obtained from rotary bending fatigue tests conducted on aged 18Ni300M steel samples processed by PBF-LB from gas and water-atomized batches, as well as by the conventional route. The unfilled symbols on the curves for the additively manufactured materials represent data points excluded from the analysis using the power law denoted in Eq. ( 1 ). Solid lines represent the modeled curves, while dashed lines correspond to extrapolations in the infinite lifespan. Fig. 7 S–N curves for aged 18Ni300M steel samples processed via PBF-LB from two powder batches and by the conventional route. Unfilled symbols indicate data points that were excluded from the fitting analysis

To obtain further insight into the particles present in the microstructure of the aged material processed from the WA batch, an area located between the crack propagation and final fracture regions, highlighted in Fig.  9 (g), was analyzed using XEDS. The results are presented in Fig.  10 (a)-(e). Fig. 10 ( a ) Region located at the boundary between the crack propagation and final fracture zones shown in Fig.  9 (g) of an aged 18Ni300M steel specimen processed from the WA batch, highlighting compositional differences among ( b ) the matrix, ( c ) a small inclusion, ( d ) powder particles, and ( e ) a large inclusion

The analysis reveals that the powder particles exhibit a chemical composition similar to that of the matrix. However, the inclusions are oxygen-rich, with smaller inclusions enriched in aluminum and iron, while the larger inclusions are primarily composed of iron and titanium.

Figure  11  presents the IPF maps of the diametral sections longitudinal to the fracture surfaces of 18Ni300M steel samples, aiming to identify the presence and propagation paths of secondary fatigue microcracks. In Fig.  11 (a) and (e), it can be observed that the secondary microcracks on the fracture profile, obtained from the sectioning of the samples, are relatively small compared to the overall extent of the microstructure along the y-axis. The crack length is even shorter in the GA-processed condition, and the grains in this microstructure are finer than those in the 18Ni300M steel processed by VIM/VAR. Figure  11 (d) shows a second-phase particle embedded in the WA fracture surface, enriched in oxygen, aluminum, titanium, and silicon, as identified by XEDS mapping. In the same figure, SEM analysis reveals cracks and decohesion between this inclusion and the matrix. Fig. 11 IPF maps of diametral sections longitudinal to the fracture surface and SEM images captured from the analysis region: ( a ) and ( b ) GA, ( c ) and ( d ) WA, and ( e ) and ( f ) VIM/VAR. An XEDS map was added for the WA condition to determine the composition of an inclusion. FS: direction parallel to the fracture surface; TD: transverse direction to the fracture surface; BD or RD: parallel direction to the build or rolling directions, respectively

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: The IPF maps shown in Fig.  2 (a) and (b) reveal the prior austenite grain structure present in the as-built microstructures of the GA and WA batches. This observation is expected, as prior austenite grain boundaries are retained in martensitic steels regardless of the cooling rate, given that martensite forms via a diffusionless transformation from austenite [ 50 ]. However, due to the extremely high cooling rates associated with the PBF-LB process, e.g., on the order of 10 5  K/s [ 14 ], the prior austenite grains are refined, and the resulting martensite exhibits cellular subgrain structures rather than the conventional hierarchical packet-block-lath morphology typically observed in martensitic steels [ 51 ]. These features are consistent with previous investigations into the microstructural characteristics of PBF-LB-processed maraging steels, such as those reported in [ 51 ]. In contrast, the microstructure of the conventionally processed alloy, shown in Fig.  2 (c), displays martensite in a blocky-lath morphology within coarser prior austenite grains.

The microstructures of the material processed from the GA and WA batches in the as-built and aged states, shown in Fig.  2 (d), (e), (g), and (h), are similar, featuring solidification cells enriched with metallic elements that segregated at the boundaries during solidification [ 11 ]. The aging temperature of 480 ºC does not dissolve these cells but primarily promotes the precipitation of nanometric intermetallics that strengthen the alloy [ 4 ]. The key difference between the GA and WA batch microstructures is the higher quantity of pores, powder particles, and inclusions in the water-atomized material. In the previous study conducted by our group [ 25 ], these inclusions were associated with metallic oxides in the microstructure, as confirmed by the XEDS maps shown in Fig.  3 (a)-(c). The oxides present in the microstructure of the WA batch in both the as-built and aged states are rich in aluminum, silicon, and titanium. Among the elements combined with oxygen, titanium is the most critical for forming the primary precipitate phases responsible for material hardening. The previously cited reference indicated that the free titanium content in the bulk processed from the WA batch was lower than in the GA batch [ 25 ], as shown in Table  1  of the present article, consistent with the high concentration of titanium-containing oxides dispersed throughout the microstructure. To determine whether aluminum, silicon, and titanium oxides were present in the material processed from the GA batch and subsequently aged, the microstructure was investigated through SEM and XEDS techniques at higher magnifications until nanometric oxides with a particle diameter of 10 1  nm [ 8 ,  52 ] were identified. By drawing a profile line across these particles, peaks of aluminum and oxygen were detected at a distance from the origin corresponding to the approximate location of one of the nanoparticles, as shown in Fig.  3 (d) and (e). According to the literature and Table  1 , since the oxygen concentration in the parts fabricated from the GA batch was considerably lower than that in the WA batch [ 53 ], the available oxygen for nano-oxide formation during PBF-LB processing is reduced, which explains the smaller size of the particles found in the GA microstructure. Confirming the presence of elements such as silicon and titanium within the particles was challenging. This limitation arises from the interaction volume associated with SEM/XEDS, which may generate compositional signals originating from multiple phases rather than a particle, affecting spatial resolution and phase distinction [ 54 ,  55 ]. To further investigate the chemical composition of the matrix and the nanoparticles, TEM and XEDS experiments were conducted, as shown in Fig.  4 . Figure  4 (a), (b), and (e) display HAADF micrographs, which reveal the presence of circular-section nanoparticles dispersed throughout the analyzed lamella. The circularity, volume fraction (V V ), and average particle diameter ( d ) were determined using ImageJ freeware [ 27 ], assuming a normal size distribution, and are presented in Table  4 . Analysis of Table  4  reveals that the particles exhibit a circularity of nearly 1.00, which is consistent with the morphology observed in the micrographs presented in Fig.  4 (a), (b), and (e). Additionally, the volume fraction is significant, especially when compared to the results of Niu et al. [ 9 ], which show that the strengthening precipitates reached a volume fraction of approximately 0.15 after 96 h of aging at 480 ºC. The average particle diameter is larger than the typical size range of precipitates in 18Ni300M steel, which generally varies from a few nanometers up to about ten nanometers [ 9 ]. Furthermore, the standard deviation associated with the average diameter is considerable, and this dispersion is visible in the TEM micrographs. Table 4 Parameters determined for the nanoparticles dispersed in the microstructure of aged 18Ni300M steel lamella processed from the GA batch 18Ni300M steel condition Circularity V V d  ( nm ) Aged PBF-LB-GA 0.97 0.27 29.5 ± 13.4

As exhibited in Fig.  4 (c), (d), and (f), the matrix presents regions of segregation of molybdenum, nickel, and titanium, as indicated by peaks in atomic fraction along the line scan shown in Fig.  4 (c) and quantified in Fig.  4 (d). These results suggest the possible presence of typical intermetallic precipitates found in 18Ni300M steel. However, confirmation of such phases would require higher magnifications, thinner lamellae, and complementary TEM techniques, such as selected area electron diffraction (SAED), which are beyond the scope of this study but have been explored in other research [ 10 ,  11 ,  56 ]. On the other hand, the circular-section nanoparticles were characterized and found to be rich in titanium, aluminum, and oxygen, as depicted in Fig.  4 (f). These elements were distributed such that aluminum and oxygen were concentrated in the particle core, while titanium was predominantly located at the outer shell. Furthermore, Fig.  4 (g) reveals that titanium peaks at the particle boundaries coincide with the outermost regions of the line profile. At the same time, aluminum and oxygen maintain relatively constant concentrations across the core and decrease at the edges. This core–shell distribution has previously been associated with nano-oxides in 18Ni300M steel processed by PBF-LB [ 46 ,  48 ], which aligns with the findings of the present study.

By comparing the Orowan stress generated by the dispersion of nano-oxides in the aged 18Ni300M steel processed with the GA batch with the yield strength of the martensitic matrix, as shown in Table  5 , a 11% increase is observed. On the other hand, the YS for this condition, as experimentally determined, is approximately 1761 MPa, as exhibited in Table  3 . When compared to the strength of the martensitic matrix, this represents an increase of about 169%. Of this strengthening contribution, the presence of aluminum and titanium-rich nano-oxides accounts for only 7%, indicating that the primary strengthening mechanism in this material is the coherent and semi-coherent precipitation of intermetallic phases such as Ni 3 Ti, Ni 3 Mo, and Laves [ 11 ,  57 ]. In the study by Mei et al. [ 11 ], the strengthening effect of Ni 3 Ti precipitates was evaluated using a model similar to the one applied. The authors reported an Orowan stress of 1970 MPa, while the experimentally determined yield strength was 1771 MPa, supporting the hypothesis that intermetallic precipitation is the dominant strengthening mechanism in maraging 300 steel. Moreover, the result suggests that nano-oxides, rather than strengthening the material due to their high hardness, contribute more to the loss of ductility observed compared to the alloy processed via the VIM/VAR route.

Analysis of the engineering stress–strain curves shown in Fig.  5  and the mechanical properties summarized in Table  3  indicates that aging increases mechanical strength and reduces ductility in the GA and VIM/VAR conditions. In contrast, a reduction in both strength and ductility occurred in the WA batch after the same heat treatment. The average curve from the three tests conducted on aged WA samples reveals that there is no plasticity in the mechanical behavior, as fracture occurs prematurely within the elastic regime. Consequently, YS could not be determined for this condition, and UTS was approximated as the fracture stress of the material. On the other hand, hardness measurements of the aged WA material were nearly identical to those of the GA batch processed by PBF-LB and the VIM/VAR conventionally fabricated material, as summarized in Table  3 . This finding indirectly confirmed that the heat treatment promoted the formation of strengthening nanoprecipitates. Yet, the enhancement in strength inevitably comes at the expense of ductility and fracture toughness [ 38 ]. According to linear elastic fracture mechanics (LEFM), the critical size of a defect can be estimated as the square of the fracture toughness divided by the yield strength, multiplied by the inverse of π. It reflects the balance between the resistance to crack propagation and the applied stress [ 38 ]. Solely for comparative purposes, considering the YS of 939 ± 3 MPa for the WA as-built condition and the experimental YS of 1761 ± 39 MPa obtained for the PBF-LB GA aged batch (assuming that the WA aged condition would be expected to attain a comparable value if significant microscopic raisers were not present with substantial size and volume fraction), and using the average fracture toughness (K Ic ) reported for 18Ni300M steel produced by PBF-LB under similar conditions to the present study [ 58 ,  59 ], 151 MPa·m 0.5  and 47 MPa·m 0.5  for the as-built and aged states, respectively, the estimated critical defect size is 8 mm for the as-built condition and 225 μm after aging. Although this estimation assumes a perfectly sharp crack in a specimen loaded in mode I, it highlights the role of precipitation in increasing internal lattice stresses and, consequently, reducing plasticity. In the case of aged samples from the WA batch, an additional detrimental factor is the presence of metallic oxides associated with the higher oxygen content detected in this condition, see Table  1 , as well as powder particles and pores, i.e., stress concentrators, dispersed throughout the microstructure, as observed on the fracture surface shown in Fig.  8 (g). Based on principles of stereology [ 60 ] and ImageJ analysis [ 27 ], Fig.  12  was prepared. Fig. 12 ( a ) Fracture surface of an aged sample from the WA batch, extracted from Fig.  8 (g), highlighting the distribution of defects. The area enclosed by the rectangle, magnified in ( b ), was analyzed using quantitative stereology, as shown in ( c ), to determine the equivalent diameter of the defects and their surface fraction. A particle located within the analyzed region was further magnified in ( d ), revealing severe localization of plastic deformation at the particle–matrix interface, leading to decohesion, delamination, and microcrack formation

The fatigue behavior of aged 18Ni300M steel specimens processed through PBF-LB using gas and water-atomized powders, and the conventional VIM/VAR route, was analyzed using the power law exhibited in Eq. ( 1 ). Data extracted from the experiments are plotted in Fig.  7 . The results from modeling S–N curves are presented in Table  6 . According to Table  6 , fatigue parameters calculated for the aged GA batch fall within an intermediate range compared to the aged WA and VIM/VAR conditions. While the material processed via the conventional VIM/VAR route and heat-treated exhibits a high  A  value, this parameter is the lowest for the aged WA batch among the three conditions, mainly due to the presence of stress concentrators [ 61 ] and a complex state of residual stresses inherited from the PBF-LB process [ 62 ]. This aligns with the microstructural analyses performed and the deterioration in tensile behavior observed for this batch. Regarding the  b  values, this parameter is nearly identical for both 18Ni300M steel batches processed by PBF-LB. In contrast,  b  assumes a higher absolute value for samples produced via the VIM/VAR route. However, as previously mentioned, the stresses applied during the rotary bending fatigue tests for the conventionally processed material were higher than those used in the tests for the alloy processed by AM from both batches. This explains the steeper decline in fatigue strength observed for the VIM/VAR condition as stress levels increase.

To compare the results of this study with others reported in the literature, S–N curves were plotted using the power law parameters determined for each of the three aged 18Ni300M steel conditions, alongside curves extracted from data of the papers of Croccolo et al. [ 23 ], Damon et al. [ 63 ], cited in Solberg et al.’s article [ 34 ], and Van Swam et al. [ 21 ], as shown in Fig.  13 . The fatigue parameters determined from the literature data were included at the end of Table  6 . Fig. 13 S–N curves modeled using a fatigue power law for the three aged 18Ni300M steel conditions investigated in this study, along with additional curves extracted from the literature

Although some of the cited studies conducted fatigue tests under axial loading and others under rotary bending, the purpose of the comparison was to evaluate whether the power law parameters fall within the same order of magnitude. It is acknowledged that, in axial fatigue tests, the entire gauge volume is subjected to stress, which can amplify the influence of internal defects. In contrast, rotary bending tests concentrate the stresses near the surface, thereby enhancing the role of surface properties.

In the study by Croccolo et al. [ 23 ], the specimens were produced using the PBF-LB process and subjected to aging at 490 ºC for 6 h, followed by air cooling. The fatigue tests were conducted under four-point rotary bending with a load ratio of R = − 1 and a frequency of 60 Hz. In Damon et al.’s research [ 63 ], the fatigue samples were also prepared using the PBF-LB technique, heat-treated at 490 ºC for 6 h, and polished with a nonwoven web to remove oxides. The specimens were submitted to cyclic tension–compression fatigue tests under a load ratio of R = − 1 and a frequency of 50 Hz. Table  6  reveals that the parameter  A  of the 18Ni300M steel in Croccolo et al. and Damon et al.’s papers is closer to that of the material processed from the WA batch and aged in the present study. Compared to conventionally fabricated maraging steel, the authors attributed the reduced fatigue strength observed in the PBF-LB-processed material to processing defects such as voids and Ti and Al-rich oxide inclusions, which served as preferential crack initiation sites. Similar defects and particles were identified in the microstructure of the samples processed from the water-atomized powder in this article.

The curve extracted from Van Swam et al.’s paper [ 21 ] depicted in Fig.  13  corresponds to tests conducted on 18Ni300M steel processed via the vacuum melting route, annealed at 820 ºC for 1 h and air-cooled, then aged at 480 ºC for 3 h and air-cooled. Tension–compression fatigue tests (R = − 1) were performed at 30 Hz. It can be observed that the modeled curve from Van Swam et al.’s paper is similar to the curve determined for the PBF-LB-GA aged 18Ni300M steel in this study. The annealing heat treatment conducted by Van Swam et al. promotes stress relief and dissolution of second-phase particles, which can reduce fatigue strength, although it enables the strength to remain relatively stable for up to 10 7  cycles. Furthermore, beyond 10 5  cycles, the fatigue strength of Van Swam et al.’s conventionally processed material surpasses that of the aged material processed from the GA powder. This may occur because the defects associated with PBF-LB processing become increasingly significant under higher stress levels, reducing the fatigue strength of the GA batch. Finally, the conventionally processed and aged 18Ni300M steel in this study cannot be directly compared with any of the conditions for which data were extracted from the literature, as evidenced by the curves shown in Fig.  13  and the parameters presented in Table  6 . It is worth noting that for metallic materials, the typical range for  b  is − 0.12 <  b  < − 0.05. Although  A , when determined from axial fatigue tests using Basquin’s law, can approximate the true fracture stress corrected for necking and obtained from monotonic tests, it is a parameter highly sensitive to the slope  b  of the S–N curve. In the case of the aged VIM/VAR condition, whose specimens were tested by rotary bending fatigue, the curve exhibits a steep decline, indicated by the largest magnitude of  b . Mathematically, maintaining this steep slope forces the curve to intersect the stress axis at an unrealistically large value of  A . Therefore, in this context, the high  A  value should be interpreted as an overestimation rather than a physical property of the material. In other words, in the low-cycle region, the microstructural characteristics of the material and the fact that the nominal stress exceeds the yield strength, leading to generalized rather than localized plastic deformation, cannot be neglected when describing fatigue resistance [ 37 ].

Figure  10 (a)-(e) provide an analysis of the chemical heterogeneity observed among the particles in the fracture surface of the aged fatigue 18Ni300M steel specimens processed from the WA batch. The surface from which fatigue cracks propagate contains microscopic constituents, including small and large inclusions, powder particles inherited from the PBF-LB process, and the martensitic matrix. Analysis of Fig.  10 (b) and (d) indicates that the chemical composition of the matrix is nearly identical to that of the analyzed powder particle. This finding confirms that some particles, which should have melted and solidified to form the component layers, remained trapped, compromising the mechanical performance of WA 18Ni300M steel. Additionally, the XEDS map of the slight inclusion shown in Fig.  10 (c) revealed a calcium peak near the Kα energy of 3.69 eV. This contamination is likely associated with the water atomization process [ 53 ], which, despite its lower cost compared to gas atomization [ 67 ], produces powders with reduced purity [ 68 ]. Initially, it may be assumed that the inclusions have a similar composition; however, the XEDS analysis reveals a key difference in the distribution of aluminum and titanium. Smaller inclusions, as shown in Fig.  10 (c), are rich in aluminum, while larger inclusions, depicted in Fig.  10 (e), are predominantly composed of titanium. Regardless of whether the inclusions are enriched in aluminum or titanium, both elements tend to form hard and brittle oxides that exhibit poor interfacial bonding with the matrix, thereby promoting premature crack initiation and accelerated crack propagation. Moreover, due to the mismatch in mechanical properties between these particles and the surrounding martensitic matrix, localized stress fields are generated even under elastic loading, which reduces the overall plasticity. Although titanium oxide with a TiO 2  stoichiometry exhibits lower hardness (624 kg·mm −2 ) than aluminum oxide (Al 2 O 3 , 2160 kg·mm −2 ) [ 69 ], Murakami’s findings [ 20 ,  70 ] indicate that the largest inclusion within the stressed volume governs the fatigue failure. Therefore, it is suggested that the larger size of titanium-rich inclusions impacts more extensive microstructure regions than aluminum-rich inclusions, thereby making the material globally more susceptible to brittle fracture. Moreover, this further supports the observed reduction in titanium content in the material processed from the WA batch compared to the GA one, as previously verified in our earlier research [ 25 ] and reported in Table  1 . This compositional variation within the inclusions leads to particles with differing hardness compared to the martensitic matrix, thereby promoting decohesion.

The EBSD analysis of secondary microcracks in the longitudinal fracture surfaces of fatigue tests for 18Ni300M steel processed through different methods is shown in Fig.  11 . In the GA condition, represented in Fig.  11 (a) and (b), the fracture surface exhibits secondary microcracks propagating through the microstructure, as indicated by the arrows. This suggests that the grains in the GA sample are susceptible to crack formation under cyclic loading. These secondary microcracks indicate that the material dissipates energy during the fatigue test, contributing to a more controlled progression of damage [ 71 ]. The behavior aligns with the improved fatigue resistance observed in the GA powder-processed parts compared to the WA condition.

In contrast, the water-atomized condition, whose results are shown in Fig.  11 (c) and (d), displays a fracture surface with no pronounced secondary microcracks initiating at the edge, based on the section analyzed. The microstructure contains inclusions, as confirmed by XEDS maps in Fig.  11 (d), highlighting elements such as oxygen, aluminum, silicon, and titanium, which serve as stress raiser sites for crack growth. Additionally, the fracture edge of the WA sample appears considerably flatter than those of the other two conditions, indicating that brittle micromechanisms are at work. The larger size of the WA defects, highlighted within the outlined region on the lower edge, suggests that they may expand in the area as the deformation progresses. Besides that, secondary microcracks are likely absent in this section due to the primary crack finding paths of considerable brittleness, such as regions containing inclusions, powder particles, and pores, as previously discussed. It is worth noting that the IPF maps of the AM-processed materials reveal a highly refined martensitic microstructure, which impairs the identification of intergranular or transgranular crack path mechanisms.

On the contrary, the VIM/VAR-processed material displays secondary microcracks that propagate in transgranular (dashed arrows) and intergranular (double-dashed arrows) modes within a more well-defined martensitic microstructure than the AM conditions, as depicted in Fig.  11 (e). The effective resistant area at the fracture edges of the VIM/VAR sample is greater than that of the GA sample, despite exhibiting irregular fracture surfaces, suggesting a more functional action of ductile micromechanisms during the cyclic loading.

In view of the significant differences observed in the microstructural and mechanical responses of components processed by PBF-LB using gas-atomized and water-atomized powder batches, a brief discussion on the atomization routes is warranted, particularly in terms of processing costs and their impact on the properties of the fabricated components. In the literature, there are categorical statements indicating that water atomization is not suitable for reactive materials such as titanium, and that steel is the most commonly water-atomized material; nevertheless, the low cost and simplicity of the process are often cited as arguments supporting its continued investigation, at least within an academic context [ 72 ]. However, the results of the present study indicate that an apparent reduction in raw material cost may ultimately lead to inferior performance, especially when PBF-LB is employed using water-atomized powders and when the material, despite being an ultra-high-strength steel, is embrittled by the presence of metallic oxides.

In this sense, literature suggests that, although gas-atomized powders are more expensive in terms of feedstock, they provide overall economic advantages, including reduced energy consumption, improved process stability, enhanced dimensional repeatability, and superior mechanical reliability. These factors justify their widespread adoption in high-precision fields, including medical, electronic, aerospace, and tooling industries [ 73 ], the latter two of which are particularly relevant to maraging steel applications. Conversely, components produced from water-atomized powders may still find application in cost-sensitive scenarios, such as non-structural parts, prototypes, or components with lower mechanical performance requirements, where economic considerations prevail over stringent reliability demands.
